blocks.text: Consider the function \(f : \mathbb{R} \to [-1, 1]\) define by \(f(x) = \sin x\). The graph of the function is shown in Figure 9.1.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "define by". It should read "defined by": consider the function \(f : \mathbb{R} \to [-1, 1]\) defined by \(f(x) = \sin x\). (The same slip is repeated at the start of 9.1.2 and 9.1.3.)

blocks.alt: Graph of y = sin x from minus 4 pi to 4 pi. The wave rises to 1 and falls to minus 1 again and again; dashed horizontal lines y = 1 and y = minus 1 touch it at every maximum and minimum point.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.1: Graph of f(x) = sin x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: Clearly the graph of the sine function is not bijective because it touches the line \(y = 1\) and \(y = -1\) at many points, due to the domain of the sine function, which is the set of all real numbers. However, if we restrict the domain of \(f(x) = \sin x\) to the closed interval \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), then the function with restricted domain, i.e., \(f : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \to [-1, 1]\), becomes one-one and onto (bijective), that is invertible, and is called the principal sine function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read Figure 9.1 with the horizontal line test: the line \(y = 1\) touches the curve at \(\dots, -\frac{7\pi}{2}, -\frac{3\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{2}, \dots\), i.e. infinitely many times, so sine on \(\mathbb{R}\) is not one-to-one. (Strictly, it is the function, not its graph, that is or is not bijective; the graph is how we see it.)
Why exactly \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)?
1. On this interval sine increases steadily from \(-1\) to \(1\), so it takes every value of \([-1, 1]\) exactly once: one-to-one and onto.
2. It contains \(0\) and all the acute angles \(0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\) that we use most.
3. Negative values of \(x\) are covered by the negative angles \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta < 0\).
Then the inverse sine function is defined by

blocks.text_alt: y equals sine inverse of x if and only if x equals sine of y

blocks.text: where the domain of \(\sin^{-1} x\) is \([-1, 1]\) and the range of \(\sin^{-1} x\) is \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

blocks.caption: Domain and range swap places (our summary)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
So \(\sin^{-1} x\) makes sense only for \(-1 \le x \le 1\): \(\sin^{-1} 2\) does not exist, because no angle has sine 2.
And whatever \(x\) is, the answer \(\sin^{-1} x\) must lie between \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). This is the test for every answer: \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6}\), never \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\), although \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\) too.

The graph of the function \(\sin : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \to [-1, 1]\) is shown in Figure 9.2(a), and the graph of \(\sin^{-1} : [-1, 1] \to \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) is shown in Figure 9.2(b).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = sin x only from minus pi over 2 to pi over 2. It rises steadily from the point (minus pi over 2, minus 1) through the origin to the point (pi over 2, 1).
blocks.caption: Figure 9.2(a): Graph of y = sin x from −π/2 to π/2 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of y = inverse sine of x from minus 1 to 1. It rises from the point (minus 1, minus pi over 2) through the origin to the point (1, pi over 2), steep at both ends.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.2(b): Graph of y = sin⁻¹ x from −1 to 1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Compare the two end points: \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)\) on the sine graph becomes \(\left(1, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) on the inverse sine graph, and \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, -1\right)\) becomes \(\left(-1, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Every point \((a, b)\) of \(y = \sin x\) gives the point \((b, a)\) of \(y = \sin^{-1} x\): the coordinates swap.
The table below gives some points of Figure 9.2(b). Each value comes from a standard angle read backwards, e.g. \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) gives \(\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\pi}{3}\).

blocks.caption: Some values of the principal inverse sine (our table; every value lies in [−π/2, π/2])

blocks.text: The graph of \(\sin^{-1} x\) is also obtain by reflecting the graph of the principal sine function \(y = \sin x\) along the line \(y = x\) as a mirror image, shown in Figure 9.3. Observe that the graph of \(y = \sin x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\).
book_errors: Observe that the graph of \(y = \sin x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "is also obtain by reflecting"; it should be "is also obtained by reflecting". It then prints "Observe that the graph of \(y = \sin x\) is symmetric about the line \(y = x\)". The graph of \(y = \sin x\) on its own is not symmetric about \(y = x\). The correct statement is: the graphs of \(y = \sin x\) (principal) and \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) are symmetric about the line \(y = x\), i.e. each is the mirror image of the other in that line.

blocks.alt: The principal sine curve from (minus pi over 2, minus 1) to (pi over 2, 1) and the inverse sine curve from (minus 1, minus pi over 2) to (1, pi over 2), drawn together with the dashed line y = x. Each curve is the mirror image of the other in that line.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.3: y = sin x and y = sin⁻¹ x are mirror images in the line y = x (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why a mirror in \(y = x\)? Reflecting a point \((a, b)\) in the line \(y = x\) gives \((b, a)\), which is exactly the swap of coordinates noted above. So the graph of any inverse function is the reflection of the graph of the function in \(y = x\).
Notice in Figure 9.3 that both curves pass through the origin and touch the line \(y = x\) there; near \(0\), \(\sin x \approx x\) and \(\sin^{-1} x \approx x\).

The sine function can be restricted to any one of the infinitely many intervals \(\left[-\frac{3\pi}{2}, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\left[\frac{3\pi}{2}, \frac{5\pi}{2}\right]\), or generally \(\left[n\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}, n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\), with range \([-1, 1]\) and length of each interval \(\pi\), where it is strictly increasing or decreasing, to make the sine function one-to-one. If the interval is not specified, then \(\sin^{-1} x\) is a function with domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Check with Figure 9.1: on \(\left[\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right]\) sine falls from \(1\) to \(-1\) (strictly decreasing), so it is also one-to-one there and takes every value of \([-1, 1]\) once. Any such interval would give an inverse, but each would give different angles.
To avoid confusion, everyone uses the same one: \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\) (that is \(n = 0\)). The value given by it is called the principal value. In this book \(\sin^{-1} x\) always means this principal function unless another interval is stated.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The \(-1\) in \(\sin^{-1}\) is not a power; it is the name of the inverse function. The reciprocal \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\) is \(\csc x\), a completely different function.
A quick numerical check (our example, \(x = \frac{1}{2}\)): \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.5236\), but \(\frac{1}{\sin(1/2)} \approx 2.0858\) (here \(\frac{1}{2}\) is an angle in radians). The two are clearly not equal.
Contrast this with \(\sin^{2} x\), which does mean \((\sin x)^{2}\). Only the index \(-1\) has this special meaning. To write the reciprocal, use \((\sin x)^{-1}\) or \(\csc x\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Principal sine function: \(\sin : \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \to [-1, 1]\), which is bijective.
2. \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) iff \(x = \sin y\), with domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
3. \(\sin^{-1} x\) exists only for \(-1 \le x \le 1\), and its value always lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
4. The graph of \(y = \sin^{-1} x\) is the mirror image of the principal sine graph in the line \(y = x\): \((a, b)\) becomes \((b, a)\).
5. \(\sin^{-1} x\) is not \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{2} = \frac{5\pi}{6}\): \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) is outside \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so it is not the principal value.
2. Writing \(\sin^{-1}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{7\pi}{6}\) or \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\): the answer must be the negative angle \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\).
3. Trying to find \(\sin^{-1} 2\) or \(\sin^{-1}(-1.5)\): these do not exist, since the domain is \([-1, 1]\).
4. Reading \(\sin^{-1} x\) as \(\frac{1}{\sin x}\).
